claim: Certain mutations affecting central metabolism cause accumulation of the oncometabolite D-2-hydroxyglutarate.
source: Certain mutations affecting central metabolism cause accumulation of the oncometabolite D-2-hydroxyglutarate which promotes progression of certain tumors.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about D-2-hydroxyglutarate and is supported by the broader scientific literature.

claim: D-2-hydroxyglutarate promotes progression of certain tumors.
source: Certain mutations affecting central metabolism cause accumulation of the oncometabolite D-2-hydroxyglutarate which promotes progression of certain tumors.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is consistent with established knowledge about oncometabolites.

claim: High levels of D-2-hydroxyglutarate inhibit the TET family of DNA demethylases.
source: High levels of D-2-hydroxyglutarate inhibit the TET family of DNA demethylases and Jumonji family of histone demethylases and cause epigenetic changes that lead to altered gene expression.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: High levels of D-2-hydroxyglutarate inhibit the Jumonji family of histone demethylases.
source: High levels of D-2-hydroxyglutarate inhibit the TET family of DNA demethylases and Jumonji family of histone demethylases and cause epigenetic changes that lead to altered gene expression.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: High levels of D-2-hydroxyglutarate cause epigenetic changes that lead to altered gene expression.
source: High levels of D-2-hydroxyglutarate inhibit the TET family of DNA demethylases and Jumonji family of histone demethylases and cause epigenetic changes that lead to altered gene expression.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Saccharomyces cerevisiae has histone demethylases but not DNA methylases or demethylases.
source: To determine whether D-2-hydroxyglutarate can affect gene expression through inhibiting histone demethylases, orthologous mutations to those known to cause accumulation of D-2-hydroxyglutarate in tumors were generated in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, which has histone demethylases but not DNA methylases or demethylases.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is established knowledge about yeast biology.

claim: Accumulation of D-2-hydroxyglutarate caused inhibition of several histone demethylases in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
source: Accumulation of D-2-hydroxyglutarate caused inhibition of several histone demethylases.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing increased histone methylation in mutants that accumulate D2-HG.

claim: Inhibition of two demethylases that act specifically on histone H3K36me2,3 led to enhanced gene silencing.
source: Inhibition of two of the demethylases that act specifically on histone H3K36me2,3 led to enhanced gene silencing.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing that gis1Δ and rph1Δ mutants phenocopy the silencing effects of D2-HG accumulation.

claim: Specific IDH mutations are highly prevalent in 60–90% of gliomas and secondary glioblastomas.
source: Specific IDH mutations are highly prevalent features of certain subsets of cancers, including 60–90% of gliomas and secondary glioblastomas, 20% of late-stage acute myelogenous leukemia, ~50% of central and periosteal cartilagenous tumors, and 10–20% of interhepatic cholangiocarcinoma (Parsons et al., 2008; Molenaar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the prevalence data.

claim: Specific IDH mutations are highly prevalent in 20% of late-stage acute myelogenous leukemia.
source: Specific IDH mutations are highly prevalent features of certain subsets of cancers, including 60–90% of gliomas and secondary glioblastomas, 20% of late-stage acute myelogenous leukemia, ~50% of central and periosteal cartilagenous tumors, and 10–20% of interhepatic cholangiocarcinoma (Parsons et al., 2008; Molenaar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the prevalence data.

claim: Specific IDH mutations are highly prevalent in ~50% of central and periosteal cartilagenous tumors.
source: Specific IDH mutations are highly prevalent features of certain subsets of cancers, including 60–90% of gliomas and secondary glioblastomas, 20% of late-stage acute myelogenous leukemia, ~50% of central and periosteal cartilagenous tumors, and 10–20% of interhepatic cholangiocarcinoma (Parsons et al., 2008; Molenaar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the prevalence data.

claim: Specific IDH mutations are highly prevalent in 10–20% of interhepatic cholangiocarcinoma.
source: Specific IDH mutations are highly prevalent features of certain subsets of cancers, including 60–90% of gliomas and secondary glioblastomas, 20% of late-stage acute myelogenous leukemia, ~50% of central and periosteal cartilagenous tumors, and 10–20% of interhepatic cholangiocarcinoma (Parsons et al., 2008; Molenaar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the prevalence data.

claim: The high frequency and patterns of IDH mutations suggest that they are important in early tumor development.
source: The high frequency and patterns of IDH mutations suggest that they are important in early tumor development.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed patterns of IDH mutations in cancers.

claim: IDH mutations contribute to progression of acute myelogenous leukemia tumors.
source: In the case of acute myelogenous leukemia, IDH mutations also contribute to progression of these tumors (Molenaar et al., 2014; Reitman and Yan, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: IDH mutations in tumors occur exclusively as heterozygous missense mutations with rare exception.
source: With rare exception, IDH mutations in tumors occur exclusively as heterozygous missense mutations.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by the broader cancer genomics literature.

claim: The most frequently documented IDH mutations occur as substitutions of arginine 132 in IDH1 or the equivalent arginine (172) in IDH2.
source: The most frequently documented IDH mutations occur as substitutions of arginine 132 in IDH1 or the equivalent arginine (172) in IDH2.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is established knowledge about IDH mutations.

claim: Tumor-associated IDH mutations abolish the conversion of isocitrate to α-ketoglutarate.
source: Tumor-associated IDH mutations appear to abolish the conversion of isocitrate to α-ketoglutarate, and instead promote a partial reverse reaction in which α-ketoglutarate is reduced to form D-2-hydroxyglutarate (D2-HG) (Dang et al., 2009; Rendina et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Tumor-associated IDH mutations promote a partial reverse reaction in which α-ketoglutarate is reduced to form D-2-hydroxyglutarate.
source: Tumor-associated IDH mutations appear to abolish the conversion of isocitrate to α-ketoglutarate, and instead promote a partial reverse reaction in which α-ketoglutarate is reduced to form D-2-hydroxyglutarate (D2-HG) (Dang et al., 2009; Rendina et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: D2-HG is typically maintained at low levels in human cells through the activity of the enzyme D-2-hydroxyglutarate dehydrogenase (D2HGDH).
source: D2-HG is a metabolite that is typically maintained at low levels in human cells through the activity of the enzyme D-2-hydroxyglutarate dehydrogenase (D2HGDH) (Achouri et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Cellular D2-HG levels are commonly elevated in IDH-mutant tumor cells, sometimes to millimolar levels.
source: Cellular D2-HG levels are commonly elevated in IDH-mutant tumor cells, sometimes to millimolar levels (Gross et al., 2010; Dang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: The α-ketoglutarate-dependent TET family of DNA demethylases are inhibited by high levels of D2-HG in vitro and in cell culture.
source: Indeed, the α-ketoglutarate-dependent TET family of DNA demethylases and Jumonji histone demethylases are inhibited by high levels of D2-HG in vitro and in cell culture, resulting in DNA and histone hypermethylation and accompanied by changes in gene expression (Figueroa et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2011; Chowdhury et al., 2011; Lu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Jumonji histone demethylases are inhibited by high levels of D2-HG in vitro and in cell culture.
source: Indeed, the α-ketoglutarate-dependent TET family of DNA demethylases and Jumonji histone demethylases are inhibited by high levels of D2-HG in vitro and in cell culture, resulting in DNA and histone hypermethylation and accompanied by changes in gene expression (Figueroa et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2011; Chowdhury et al., 2011; Lu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Inhibition of TET and Jumonji demethylases by D2-HG results in DNA and histone hypermethylation.
source: Indeed, the α-ketoglutarate-dependent TET family of DNA demethylases and Jumonji histone demethylases are inhibited by high levels of D2-HG in vitro and in cell culture, resulting in DNA and histone hypermethylation and accompanied by changes in gene expression (Figueroa et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2011; Chowdhury et al., 2011; Lu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: AMLs tend to have either mutations in IDH or mutations in the genes encoding TET enzymes, but not both.
source: There is strong circumstantial evidence from acute myeloid leukemias (AMLs) that DNA demethylases are the targets of the D2-HG produced by the IDH mutations: AMLs tend to have either the mutations in IDH or mutations in the genes encoding TET enzymes, but not both (Figueroa et al., 2010; Gaidzik et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Elevated bulk histone methylation has been reported for some tumors producing D2-HG.
source: Indeed elevated bulk histone methylation has been reported for some tumors producing D2-HG, but whether critical changes in gene expression result from inhibition of DNA demethylation or inhibition of histone demethylation in these tumors is an important and unresolved question (Chowdhury et al., 2011; Gaidzik et al., 2012; Lu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Tumors with elevated D2-HG levels show bulk increases in histone methyl marks associated with both transcriptional activation (H3K4, H3K36) and repression (H3K9, H3K27).
source: Further, tumors with elevated D2-HG levels show bulk increases in histone methyl marks typically associated with both transcriptional activation (H3K4, H3K36) and repression (H3K9, H3K27) (Turcan et al., 2012; Lu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: The yeast and human IDH proteins share 61% amino acid identity.
source: The yeast and human proteins share 61% amino acid identity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by the alignment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The IDP2-R132H mutation is analogous to the most common mutation found in low-grade gliomas and secondary glioblastomas in the human ortholog IDH1.
source: This mutation is analogous to the most common mutation found in low-grade gliomas and secondary glioblastomas in the human ortholog IDH1 (reviewed in Waitkus et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The IDP2-R132H mutation increased the stability of heterochromatin compared to wild-type IDP2.
source: The IDP2-R132H mutation increased the stability of heterochromatin (p<0.0001; Student's t test) compared to wild-type IDP2, resulting in fewer switches from RFP to GFP expression (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The effect of IDP2-R132H on heterochromatin stability was dependent on IDP2 expression.
source: This effect was dependent on IDP2 expression, as no effect was observed when cells were plated on medium containing glucose, which represses IDP2 expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Deletion of IDP2 did not affect the stability of heterochromatin.
source: Deletion of IDP2 did not affect the stability of heterochromatin suggesting that IDP2-R132H results in a gain-of-function.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by the data in Figure 1B.

claim: IDP2-R132H results in a gain-of-function.
source: Deletion of IDP2 did not affect the stability of heterochromatin suggesting that IDP2-R132H results in a gain-of-function.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that deletion of IDP2 has no effect while the R132H mutation does.

claim: The dld2∆ mutant phenocopied the effect of the IDP2-R132H mutant and increased gene silencing compared to wild type on medium with glycerol as the sole carbon source.
source: Indeed, on medium with glycerol as the sole carbon source, when oxidative phosphorylation is the primary means of ATP production, the dld2∆ mutant phenocopied the effect of the IDP2-R132H mutant and increased gene silencing compared to wild type (p<0.0001; Student's t test) (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: The IDP2-R132H dld2∆ double mutant resulted in a further increase in heterochromatin stability compared to wild type and dld2Δ alone.
source: Moreover, the IDP2-R132H dld2∆ double mutant resulted in a further increase in heterochromatin stability compared to wild type (p<0.0001; Student's t test) and dld2Δ alone (p<0.05; Student's t test) (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: A dld3∆ mutation did not increase heterochromatin stability when cells were grown on glycerol medium.
source: A dld3∆ mutation did not increase heterochromatin stability when cells were grown on glycerol medium (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1F,G.

claim: Both dld2∆ and dld3∆ mutations led to increased heterochromatin stability when cells were grown on glucose.
source: However, when cells were grown on glucose, where ATP is primarily generated through sugar fermentation, both dld2∆ and dld3∆ mutations led to increased heterochromatin stability (Figure 1H,I).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1H,I.

claim: D2-HG is normally produced in yeast.
source: The increase in heterochromatin stability in the dld2∆ and dld3∆ mutants implied that D2-HG is normally produced in yeast under these and other conditions (see also Becker-Kettern et al., 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that deletion of D2-HG dehydrogenases leads to increased silencing, implying that D2-HG is normally present and metabolized.

claim: The IDP2-R132H allele is dominant to wild-type IDP2.
source: In an IPD2-R132H/IDP2 heterozygous diploid strain, gene silencing was increased compared to the equivalent strain with two copies of wild-type IDP2 (Figure 2A,B), demonstrating that the yeast mutation, analogous to the cancer-driver mutation in human IDH1, was dominant to wild-type IDP2.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: A strain homozygous for IDP2-R132H had less stable gene silencing than the heterozygous strain.
source: Interestingly, a strain homozygous for IDP2-R132H had less stable gene silencing than the heterozygous strain, suggesting that the effect of IDP2-R132H on silencing was synergistic with a wild-type copy of IDP2.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: The effect of IDP2-R132H on silencing was synergistic with a wild-type copy of IDP2.
source: Interestingly, a strain homozygous for IDP2-R132H had less stable gene silencing than the heterozygous strain, suggesting that the effect of IDP2-R132H on silencing was synergistic with a wild-type copy of IDP2.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that heterozygotes have stronger silencing than homozygotes.

claim: Knockout of the wild-type copy of IDH1 in IDH1R132H/WT tumor cell lines results in decreased D2-HG formation relative to IDH1R132H/WT cells.
source: These results echoed the observation in IDH1R132H/WT tumor cell lines that knockout of the wild-type copy of IDH1 (IDH1R132H/-)  results in decreased D2-HG formation relative to IDH1R132H/WT cells (Jin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a citation to support the claim.

claim: D2-HG levels in wild-type strains ranged between 10 and 60 µM.
source: D2-HG levels in wild-type strains ranged between 10 and 60 µM, in agreement with previous levels measured in yeast (Becker-Kettern et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by LC-MS data.

claim: A dld2∆ mutation led to a ~50 fold increase in cellular D2-HG levels in cells grown on glycerol.
source: Consistent with a role in metabolizing D2-HG, a dld2∆ mutation led to a ~50 fold increase in cellular D2-HG levels in cells grown on glycerol (Figure 3A) and a fivefold increase in cells grown on glucose (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A dld2∆ mutation led to a fivefold increase in cellular D2-HG levels in cells grown on glucose.
source: Consistent with a role in metabolizing D2-HG, a dld2∆ mutation led to a ~50 fold increase in cellular D2-HG levels in cells grown on glycerol (Figure 3A) and a fivefold increase in cells grown on glucose (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: A dld3Δ mutation led to a sevenfold increase in cellular D2-HG in cells grown on glucose.
source: A dld3Δ mutation also led to a sevenfold increase in cellular D2-HG, but this increase was observed only in cells grown on glucose (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: D2-HG is efficiently metabolized by Dld2 and Dld3.
source: Thus, D2-HG is a normal feature of the S. cerevisiae metabolome and is efficiently metabolized by Dld2 and Dld3, as noted (Becker-Kettern et al., 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that deletion of these enzymes leads to D2-HG accumulation.

claim: Dld3 activity toward D2-HG was limited to cells grown on fermentable carbon sources like glucose.
source: However, Dld3 activity toward D2-HG was limited to cells grown on fermentable carbon sources like glucose.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by the differential effects of dld3Δ on D2-HG levels in glucose vs. glycerol media.

claim: The Idp2-R132H mutation contributed to D2-HG production when measured in combination with dld2∆ and wild-type Idp2 protein.
source: Although the increased D2-HG level in the Idp2-R132h mutant inferred from the silencing phenotype was not detected in the LC-MS analysis of cells that were able to metabolize it (Figure 3A), the Idp2-R132H mutation clearly contributed to D2-HG production when measured in combination with dld2∆ and wild-type Idp2 protein (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: D2-HG production by yeast Idp2-R132H was enhanced by the presence of wild-type Idp2.
source: To test whether D2-HG production by yeast Idp2-R132H was likewise enhanced by the presence of wild-type Idp2, cells were transformed with a plasmid containing a copy of the wild-type IDP2 gene expressed from its native promoter. The presence of an extra copy of wild-type IDP2 had no effect on D2-HG levels in wild-type IDP2 cells (Figure 3B, bar 3 versus bar 4). However, D2-HG levels significantly increased (p<0.05) in mutant IDP2-R132H cells when an extra copy of wild-type IDP2 was present (Figure 3B, bar 5 versus bar 4).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: An extra copy of wild-type IDP2 enhanced silencing in mutant IDP2-R132H cells compared to strains with only wild-type IDP2.
source: In parallel to the results measuring D2-HG levels, an extra copy of wild-type IDP2 enhanced silencing in mutant IDP2-R132H cells compared to strains with only wild-type IDP2 (p<0.0001; Student's t test).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is a strong correlation between D2-HG levels and increased silencing at a heterochromatic locus.
source: These results demonstrated a strong correlation between D2-HG levels and increased silencing at a heterochromatic locus.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by the combined data from D2-HG measurements and silencing assays.

claim: Treatment of dld2Δ mutant cells with octyl-D2-HG resulted in increased gene silencing compared to untreated cells.
source: However, treatment of dld2Δ mutant cells with octyl-D2-HG resulted in increased gene silencing compared to the untreated cells (p<0.05) (Figure 4B) establishing that increases in D2-HG were causal for stabilizing gene silencing.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Increases in D2-HG were causal for stabilizing gene silencing.
source: However, treatment of dld2Δ mutant cells with octyl-D2-HG resulted in increased gene silencing compared to the untreated cells (p<0.05) (Figure 4B) establishing that increases in D2-HG were causal for stabilizing gene silencing.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by the experimental manipulation of D2-HG levels using octyl-D2-HG.

claim: The impact of D2-HG did not extend to all forms of repression.
source: When dld2∆ mutations were introduced into the pGAL1::cre strain, repression of cre was maintained to the same degree as in wild type, indicating that the impact of D2-HG did not extend to all forms of repression (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Bulk levels of H3K36-mono and -trimethyl marks were significantly higher in dld2∆ IDP2-R132H strains compared to wild type.
source: Bulk levels of H3K36-mono and -trimethyl and H3K4-trimethyl marks were significantly higher (p<0.01) in dld2∆ IDP2-R132H strains compared to wild type (Figure 6A and B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Bulk levels of H3K4-trimethyl marks were significantly higher in dld2∆ IDP2-R132H strains compared to wild type.
source: Bulk levels of H3K36-mono and -trimethyl and H3K4-trimethyl marks were significantly higher (p<0.01) in dld2∆ IDP2-R132H strains compared to wild type (Figure 6A and B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: There is no known H3K79 demethylase in S. cerevisiae.
source: The lack of change in H3K79 methylation levels was consistent with this model as there is no known H3K79 demethylase in S. cerevisiae.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and is established knowledge about yeast biology.

claim: Both gis1∆ and rph1∆ single mutants enhanced gene silencing compared to wild type.
source: Indeed, both gis1∆ and rph1∆ single mutants enhanced gene silencing compared to wild type (p<0.0001; Student's t test), and the rph1∆ gis1∆ double mutants resulted in even further enhancement compared to wild type (p<0.0001; Student's t test) (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: The rph1∆ gis1∆ double mutants resulted in even further enhancement of gene silencing compared to wild type.
source: Indeed, both gis1∆ and rph1∆ single mutants enhanced gene silencing compared to wild type (p<0.0001; Student's t test), and the rph1∆ gis1∆ double mutants resulted in even further enhancement compared to wild type (p<0.0001; Student's t test) (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: The jhd1∆ mutant had no statistically significant effect on gene silencing on its own or in combination with either rph1∆ or gis1∆ mutations.
source: The jhd1∆ mutant had no statistically significant effect on its own or in combination with either rph1∆ or gis1∆ mutations, nor did ecm5∆ and jhd2∆ mutations (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Elevated H3K36 methylation was the determinant for increasing heterochromatin stability.
source: Therefore, elevated H3K36 methylation was the determinant for increasing heterochromatin stability, and Rph1 and Gis1 were implicated as the primary demethylases inhibited by D2-HG accumulation that led to enhanced heterochromatic gene silencing.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that only H3K36 demethylase mutants phenocopy the D2-HG accumulation effects.

claim: Rph1 and Gis1 were implicated as the primary demethylases inhibited by D2-HG accumulation that led to enhanced heterochromatic gene silencing.
source: Therefore, elevated H3K36 methylation was the determinant for increasing heterochromatin stability, and Rph1 and Gis1 were implicated as the primary demethylases inhibited by D2-HG accumulation that led to enhanced heterochromatic gene silencing.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic analysis showing that gis1Δ and rph1Δ mutants phenocopy D2-HG accumulation effects.

claim: GIS1 and RPH1 overexpressed from a galactose-inducible plasmid led to destabilization of heterochromatin.
source: In further support, GIS1 and RPH1 overexpressed from a galactose-inducible plasmid led to destabilization of heterochromatin (Figure 7C); in contrast, overexpression of JHD1 had no effect (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Overexpression of JHD1 had no effect on heterochromatin stability.
source: In further support, GIS1 and RPH1 overexpressed from a galactose-inducible plasmid led to destabilization of heterochromatin (Figure 7C); in contrast, overexpression of JHD1 had no effect (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Methylation of H3K36 is exclusively dependent on the methyltransferase Set2.
source: Methylation of H3K36 is exclusively dependent on the methyltransferase Set2 (Strahl et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The loss of Set2 completely abrogated the effect of gis1∆ rph1∆ on gene silencing.
source: The loss of Set2 completely abrogated the effect of gis1∆ rph1∆ on gene silencing. The extent of gene silencing in the triple mutant was no different from either wild type or set2∆ single mutants (Figure 7D,E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 7D,E.

claim: The enhanced gene silencing in gis1∆ and rph1∆ mutants was due exclusively to H3K36 hypermethylation.
source: Because set2∆ suppressed gis1∆ and rph1∆, the enhanced gene silencing in gis1∆ and rph1∆ mutants was due exclusively to H3K36 hypermethylation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that set2Δ suppresses the silencing phenotype of gis1Δ rph1Δ mutants.

claim: Gene silencing in set2Δ dld2Δ double mutants and set2Δ dld2Δ IDP2-R132H triple mutants was no different from set2Δ single mutants.
source: Indeed, gene silencing in set2Δ dld2Δ double mutants and set2Δ dld2Δ IDP2-R132H triple mutants was no different from set2Δ single mutants (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 8A,B.

claim: gis1Δ rph1Δ dld2Δ and gis1Δ rph1Δ dld2Δ IDP2-R132H mutants displayed identical levels of silencing to the gis1Δ rph1Δ double mutant.
source: This prediction was confirmed by analysis of gis1Δ rph1Δ dld2Δ and gis1Δ rph1Δ dld2Δ IDP2-R132H mutants, which displayed identical levels of silencing to the gis1Δ rph1Δ double mutant (Figure 8C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 8C,D.

claim: The elevated gene silencing observed in cells that accumulate D2-HG was due to Set2-dependent methylation of H3K36, and its subsequent hypermethylation due to inhibition of the Gis1 and Rph1 demethylases.
source: These results provided the functional confirmation that the elevated gene silencing observed in cells that accumulate D2-HG was due to Set2-dependent methylation of H3K36, and its subsequent hypermethylation due to inhibition of the Gis1 and Rph1 demethylases.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by the combined genetic analysis.

claim: Enhanced gene silencing was due to histone H3K36 hypermethylation in response to the oncometabolite D2-HG inhibiting two specific histone demethylases.
source: Here, we demonstrated unequivocally that enhanced gene silencing was due to histone H3K36 hypermethylation in response to the oncometabolite D2-HG inhibiting two specific histone demethylases.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the experimental results.

claim: D2-HG was detected in metabolite extracts even from wild-type cells.
source: D2-HG was detected in metabolite extracts even from wild-type cells, suggesting it is a normal component of the yeast metabolome.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the LC-MS data.

claim: Wild-type cells maintained D2-HG at low levels through the activity of D2-HG dehydrogenases.
source: Wild-type cells maintained D2-HG at low levels through the activity of D2-HG dehydrogenases.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that deletion of D2-HG dehydrogenases leads to D2-HG accumulation.

claim: Only Dld2 had a role in metabolizing D2-HG in vivo in cells grown on glycerol.
source: However, only Dld2 had a role in metabolizing D2-HG in vivo in cells grown on glycerol, suggesting that Dld3 and Dld2 are differentially regulated in response to the mode of energy production in the cell.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the differential effects of dld2Δ and dld3Δ on D2-HG levels in different growth conditions.

claim: Dld3 and Dld2 are differentially regulated in response to the mode of energy production in the cell.
source: However, only Dld2 had a role in metabolizing D2-HG in vivo in cells grown on glycerol, suggesting that Dld3 and Dld2 are differentially regulated in response to the mode of energy production in the cell.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Dld2 and Dld3 have different effects on D2-HG metabolism depending on the carbon source.

claim: D2-HG acts as a competitive inhibitor of human Jumonji histone demethylase enzymes.
source: D2-HG acts as a competitive inhibitor of human Jumonji histone demethylase enzymes.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is supported by the broader literature on D2-HG biochemistry.

claim: The genetic and molecular evidence strongly implied that yeast Jumonji-domain histone demethylases are biochemically inhibited by D2-HG.
source: Whether yeast Jumonji-domain histone demethylases are biochemically inhibited by D2-HG has not explicitly been tested, although the genetic and molecular evidence strongly implied such a mechanism.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is inferred from the genetic and molecular data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Increases in D2-HG were readily measured in dld2-mutants, but not in cells capable of degrading D2-HG.
source: Increases in D2-HG were readily measured in dld2-mutants, but not in cells capable of degrading D2-HG.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the LC-MS data.

claim: Accumulation of D2-HG led to hypermethylation of histone H3 at lysine 4 and lysine 36.
source: Accumulation of D2-HG led to hypermethylation of histone H3 at lysine 4 and lysine 36.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the immunoblot data.

claim: It was the loss of histone demethylases that act on H3K36 that was solely responsible for increased stabilization of heterochromatin.
source: Importantly, it was the loss of histone demethylases that act on H3K36 that was solely responsible for increased stabilization of heterochromatin.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the genetic analysis showing that only H3K36 demethylase mutants affect silencing.

claim: Inhibition of H3K4 demethylation and the resulting elevation of bulk H3K4me had no effect on gene silencing.
source: Inhibition of H3K4 demethylation and the resulting elevation of bulk H3K4me had no effect on gene silencing.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the observation that jhd2Δ mutants do not affect silencing.

claim: Methylation of H3K36 at transcribed genes prevents aberrant transcription from initiating from within the open-reading frames of actively transcribed genes.
source: Methylation of H3K36 at transcribed genes prevents aberrant transcription from initiating from within the open-reading frames of actively transcribed genes (Carrozza et al., 2005; Keogh et al., 2005; Joshi and Struhl, 2005), although this process appears to be incompatible with silencing at HML for reasons detailed below.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to support the claim.

claim: H3K4 methylation plays a role in the establishment of silencing at HML.
source: For example, H3K4 methylation occurs at the 5' ends of actively transcribed genes and is important for maintaining a local chromatin landscape conducive to transcription, and yet it also plays a role in the establishment of silencing at HML (Osborne et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Methylation of H3K79 by Dot1 inhibits Sir3-H3 interaction.
source: The site at which Sir3 interacts with histone H3 includes H3K79, and methylation of H3K79 by Dot1 inhibits Sir3-H3 interaction (Armache et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The Rpd3 complex antagonizes silencing at heterochromatic loci HML and HMR by limiting Sir3 and Sir4 occupancy at flanking silencer regions.
source: For example, the Rpd3 complex antagonizes silencing at heterochromatic loci HML and HMR by limiting Sir3 and Sir4 occupancy at flanking silencer regions (Thurtle-Schmidt et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The deacetylase activity of Rpd3(S) is directed toward nucleosomes at actively transcribed genes in part through an interaction between the Eaf3 subunit of the Rpd3(S) complex and histones methylated at H3K36.
source: Importantly, the deacetylase activity of Rpd3(S) is directed toward nucleosomes at actively transcribed genes in part through an interaction between the Eaf3 subunit of the Rpd3(S) complex and histones methylated at H3K36 (Carrozza et al., 2005; Keogh, 2005; Joshi and Struhl, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to support the claim.

claim: H3K36 methylation prevents binding of Sir proteins to heterochromatin-adjacent and telomere-adjacent regions.
source: Finally, H3K36 methylation prevents binding of Sir proteins to heterochromatin-adjacent and telomere-adjacent regions (Tompa and Madhani, 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Increased silencing of tumor suppressor genes is a feature of many tumors.
source: Increased silencing of tumor suppressor genes is a feature of many tumors.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is established knowledge about cancer biology.

claim: This study pinpointed specific histone demethylase enzymes whose inhibition by D2-HG resulted in increased gene silencing.
source: This study pinpointed specific histone demethylase enzymes whose inhibition by D2-HG resulted in increased gene silencing.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the experimental results.

claim: This study demonstrated that D2-HG enhanced gene silencing through stabilization of heterochromatic DNA.
source: Further, this study demonstrated that D2-HG enhanced gene silencing through stabilization of heterochromatic DNA.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the experimental results using the CRASH assay.

claim: IDP2 is expressed only on non-fermentable carbon sources.
source: Because IDP2 is expressed only on non-fermentable carbon sources (Haselbeck and McAlister-Henn, 1993), cells were plated on solid medium containing glycerol as the sole carbon source to induce IDP2 expression.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Tumors with the equivalent isocitrate dehydrogenase mutation (IDH1-R132H) are exclusively heterozygous, retaining a wild-type copy of IDH1.
source: Tumors with the equivalent isocitrate dehydrogenase mutation (IDH1-R132H) are exclusively heterozygous, retaining a wild-type copy of IDH1, and knock-down of wild-type IDH1 reduces D2-HG produced by IDH1-R132H (Ward et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Knock-down of wild-type IDH1 reduces D2-HG produced by IDH1-R132H.
source: Tumors with the equivalent isocitrate dehydrogenase mutation (IDH1-R132H) are exclusively heterozygous, retaining a wild-type copy of IDH1, and knock-down of wild-type IDH1 reduces D2-HG produced by IDH1-R132H (Ward et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a citation to support the claim.

claim: IDH is typically a homodimer.
source: Because IDH is typically a homodimer, presumably the wild-type enzyme provides a local source of α-ketoglutarate for the mutant enzyme to convert to D2-HG (Ward et al., 2013; Jin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and is established knowledge about IDH structure.

claim: The wild-type IDH enzyme provides a local source of α-ketoglutarate for the mutant enzyme to convert to D2-HG.
source: Because IDH is typically a homodimer, presumably the wild-type enzyme provides a local source of α-ketoglutarate for the mutant enzyme to convert to D2-HG (Ward et al., 2013; Jin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with citations to support the claim.

claim: Rph1, Gis1, and Jhd1 demethylate various species of methylated H3K36.
source: There are five known Jumonji-domain proteins in S. cerevisiae and among them Rph1, Gis1, and Jhd1 demethylate various species of methylated H3K36 (Tu et al., 2007; Kim and Buratowski, 2007) and Jhd2 demethylates mono-, di-, and trimethylated H3K4 (Seward et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with citations to support the claim.

claim: Jhd2 demethylates mono-, di-, and trimethylated H3K4.
source: There are five known Jumonji-domain proteins in S. cerevisiae and among them Rph1, Gis1, and Jhd1 demethylate various species of methylated H3K36 (Tu et al., 2007; Kim and Buratowski, 2007) and Jhd2 demethylates mono-, di-, and trimethylated H3K4 (Seward et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a citation to support the claim.
